newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU does the minimum on foreign, defence policy.
newsitem.headline: EU does the minimum on foreign, defence policy.

text.p: In a move that could have lasting consequences in world affairs, the European Union decided on Tuesday against taking bold steps towards building a common foreign and defence policy.

The 15 leaders approved a new Union treaty text for the 21st century, which gave the job of representing the EU in foreign policy to a little-known Eurocrat and made no significant move towards taking charge of their joint defence.
Diplomats said the modest result of the EU's Amsterdam summit was likely to reinforce the United States' pre-eminence in European security for years to come, diplomats said.

France and Germany, which had declared last year that Europe must have a single face and voice to run a credible foreign policy, settled in the end for making it a part-time job for the secretary-general of the EU's council of ministers.

That civil servant, who heads the policy-making council's Brussels secretariat, is currently a German diplomat named Juergen Trumpf, a former troubleshooter for Chancellor Helmut Kohl unknown to the public.

French President Jacques Chirac who had insisted earlier on Tuesday that the idea of making the council secretary-general "Monsieur PESC" (Mr Common Foreign Policy) was unacceptable, climbed down, saying the compromise responded to Paris' call.

French officials said Trumpf was nearing retirement and a higher-profile political figure might succeed him. But it is not clear that other countries, reluctant to see their own foreign ministers overshadowed, would necessarily agree to that.

The "secretary-general/high representative for common foreign and security policy" will assist the country holding the EU's rotating presidency in diplomacy and head a Brussels policy analysis and planning unit to improve crisis response.

Faced with dogged opposition from Britain and former neutral states to the EU becoming a defence organisation, the leaders were unable to agree to merge the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping into the Union.
Instead, they decided the 10-nation WEU would remain an independent body, sub-contracted to carry out humanitarian, peacekeeping and crisis management missions for the Union "including peacemaking".
The idea of eventually merging the WEU into the Union was watered down to such an extent that even Britain's staunchly Atlanticist government accepted the wording.
The text called for "closer institutional relations with the WEU with a view to the possibility of the integration of the WEU into the Union should the European Council so decide".
A clause calling for the article to be reviewed in five years' time was scrapped, as was a call for closer EU armaments cooperation.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair told reporters: "It makes it absolutely clear that our defence interests will continue to be looked at in NATO."
Greek negotiator Stellios Perrakis told reporters the agreement had been "watered down in the extreme. This is a very little agreement."

While Britain's main concern was not to weaken the American security guarantee for Europe, Ireland and three other neutral states which joined the EU in 1995 -- Sweden, Finland and Austria -- were wary about Europe becoming a military power.
Nordic countries were also concerned that getting the EU into defence could complicate the Baltic republics' bids for membership by raising Russian objections.

Swedish chief negotiator Gunnar Lund said: "We object to the basic idea of enshrining into the treaty a clear-cut objective to integrate the EU and the WEU. We don't want to see that. We find that unacceptable.
"If this were done, it would unnecessarily complicate the (EU) enlargement process. It will accentuate divisions rather than unity within the EU in this particular area."
